images.text:
Location: Laughing Cow Comedy Club

Date: Friday, November 30th

There is a lot being written about Larry Fine and his witty comedy, sharp tongue, and perfect delivery. His performance is being touted as the next big star. With these reviews in mind, I headed down to the Laughing Cow Comedy Club on Friday night for an evening of amusement. Not only did I find his humor to be disappointing, but I also thought it was very rude.

Fine's show is a mixture of insults, racist and sexist comments, and name-calling. Besides the fact that he insults almost every racial group imaginable, he has attacked and picked on vulnerable people out of the audience. Although, this show has been given so many accolades,  it represents the lowest form of comedy that exists: cheap laughs at the expense of others. His show is being promoted as something it is not. Audience members have been misguided.

Although many audience members clearly find the show hilarious, others have been hurt by the comedian. I took the opportunity to have a chat with the owner of the Laughing Cow, after the show. He clearly disagreed with me about the show and about Larry Fine himself. His explanation was that, “Larry hasn't focussed on one specific group or person; he's not racist. His show used to be more controversial. He's going straight to the top." In my opinion,  Fine has damaged the reputation of comedians. I used to love going to see comedy shows live and would pay a lot of money. What a disgrace!

Present Perfect tense vs. Past Simple and Used to and Would

You use the Present Perfect tense to talk about a finished action or event that is connected to the present in some way.
You use the Simple Past tense to talk about a finished action or event not necessarily connected to the present.

You can use the Present Perfect tense to talk about experience.
When you use the Present Perfect tense, you think about the past and present together. There is some connection between what happened in the past and now.
To help you decide whether you should use the Present Perfect tense or the Past Simple tense, ask yourself the questions ‘When?'
If you can answer the question ‘When?', the past time is stated or inferred or understood. Use the Past Simple. There is no connection to the present.
If you cannot answer the question ‘When?', because the time is not stated or not important, then choose the Present Perfect tense. There is instead a connection to the present.
Past Habit – Used to and Would
When we talk about things that happened in the past but don't happen anymore we can do it in different ways.

You can use used to to talk about past states that don't happen now.

You can also use used to to talk about repeated actions.

Example:
  • I used to go to comedy shows all the time.
  • I used to love going to these shows but I have now changed my mind.
  • His show used to be more controversial.
You can use would to talk about repeated past actions.

Example:
  • We would always sit up the front to get a better view of the stage.
  • I used to love going to see comedy shows live and would pay a lot of money.

Passive of Present Continuous tense and Present Perfect tense

You often choose the passive form when you want to talk about an action but are not so interested in saying who or what does/did it. Passives without agents (the doers) are common in academic and scientific writing.
You use the Present Continuous to talk about an action that is happening at the time of speaking. The action or event is in progress.
Passive sentences in the Present Continuous tense have the following structure:
Object of the active sentence + is/are/am + being + past participle form of the verb + by + subject of the active sentence.
You use the Present Perfect to talk about a finished action or event with present consequences. There is a connection between what happened in the past and the present.
You can use the Present Perfect passive to talk about the same kind of actions or events.
The passive shifts the focus from the doer of the action (agent) to the receiver of the action.
